terms.definition: The growing interconnectedness of societies through flows of goods, money, people, information and culture.
terms.examiner: Define it with at least two dimensions (economic, cultural, political) before evaluating.

terms.definition: The view that globalisation is real, new and largely positive, weakening nation-states.
The view that globalisation is exaggerated: most trade is still regional and nation-states remain powerful.
terms.examiner: Hirst and Thompson; a strong counter-argument in essays.

terms.definition: The view that globalisation is real but uneven, changing rather than replacing the role of nation-states.
terms.examiner: Held; useful as a middle position that reaches a judgement.

terms.definition: The sense that the world is shrinking as communication and travel speed up.
terms.examiner: Harvey; link to digital media and global markets.

terms.definition: Companies that operate in many countries and can shift production to where costs are lowest.
terms.examiner: Use them as evidence of economic globalisation and of power shifting away from states.

terms.definition: The idea that globalisation makes cultures more alike, often around Western or American models.
The adaptation of global products and ideas to local cultures.
terms.examiner: Good evidence against the homogenisation view; give a concrete example.

terms.definition: The mixing of cultures to create new forms.
terms.examiner: Pieterse; links to hybrid identities in topic 7.2.

terms.definition: Wallerstein's view of a global capitalist system divided into core, semi-periphery and periphery.
terms.examiner: A Marxist perspective on why globalisation benefits rich countries most.
